primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Congenital afibrinogenemia is a severe quantitative fibrinogen disorder, usually autosomal recessive, caused by pathogenic variants affecting fibrinogen-chain genes or fibrinogen synthesis/assembly/secretion. Near-absence of circulating fibrinogen prevents normal fibrin clot formation, causing marked prolongation of fibrin-dependent clotting assays.
vignette: A 2-week-old infant is evaluated for persistent bleeding after separation of the umbilical stump. The platelet count is normal. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and thrombin time are all markedly prolonged. A Clauss fibrinogen assay shows no detectable functional fibrinogen, and an immunologic assay shows no detectable fibrinogen antigen.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Hemophilia A causes factor VIII deficiency and typically produces an isolated prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal prothrombin time and normal fibrinogen level.

Factor XIII stabilizes fibrin after the initial clot forms. Factor XIII deficiency can cause delayed bleeding and umbilical stump bleeding, but routine PT, aPTT, and thrombin time are typically normal because these assays end before factor XIII-mediated cross-linking.
von Willebrand disease impairs platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. PT is normal and fibrinogen is not absent; aPTT may be normal or prolonged depending on factor VIII levels.

Dysfibrinogenemia is a qualitative fibrinogen defect. Functional activity is disproportionately reduced relative to antigen concentration; complete absence of both functional fibrinogen and fibrinogen antigen is characteristic of afibrinogenemia.
key_expl: The infant has congenital afibrinogenemia. The decisive laboratory pattern is undetectable fibrinogen activity and antigen together with marked prolongation of PT, aPTT, and thrombin time, all of which ultimately depend on fibrin formation. Umbilical bleeding is a classic early presentation. Hemophilia A affects the intrinsic pathway, factor XIII deficiency occurs after fibrin formation and therefore does not prolong routine clotting times, von Willebrand disease does not eliminate fibrinogen, and dysfibrinogenemia is primarily a qualitative rather than complete quantitative fibrinogen defect.
objective: Recognize congenital afibrinogenemia from early bleeding plus absent functional and antigenic fibrinogen with marked prolongation of fibrin-dependent coagulation assays.
